power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Background: Regular exercise during pregnancy improves maternal and neonatal outcomes; however, the molecular pathways underlying placental adaptations to prenatal exercise remain poorly understood.

Klotho is a cytoprotective protein involved in the regulation of oxidative stress, metabolic homeostasis, and cellular resilience, yet whether placental Klotho concentrations are associated with prenatal exercise has not been previously investigated.
Aims: The primary aim of this study was to examine whether participation in a supervised concurrent exercise program during pregnancy is associated with placental Klotho concentrations at birth.
Secondary aims were to explore potential fetal sex-specific patterns and associations between placental Klotho and selected biomarkers related to angiogenic and inflammatory pathways.
Methods: Pregnant women were allocated to either a supervised concurrent exercise program or usual care.
The intervention comprised combined aerobic and resistance training performed three times per week from early-mid pregnancy until birth.
Placental tissue was collected at birth, and Klotho concentrations were quantified by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA).
Secondary analyses explored potential sex-specific patterns and examined associations between placental Klotho, placental weight, and a panel of placental biomarkers.
Results: Seventy-six women were included (exercise: n = 41; control: n = 35).
Placental Klotho concentrations were significantly higher in the exercise group, with an adjusted mean difference of approximately 101 pg/mL (p = 0.001; partial η² = 0.164).
This effect was consistent across fetal sex, with no significant exercise-by-sex interaction.
Several placental biomarkers were independently associated with Klotho, suggesting a potential relationship with angiogenic and inflammatory signaling pathways.
Conclusions: Participation in a supervised concurrent exercise program during pregnancy is associated with higher placental Klotho concentrations at birth, irrespective of fetal sex.

These findings provide novel insight into molecular pathways potentially involved in placental adaptations associated with prenatal exercise and reinforce the concept of the placenta as an exercise-responsive organ during pregnancy.
Regular physical exercise during pregnancy is widely recognized as a key component of maternal-fetal health (1) (2) (3) (4) (5).

text.text: For instance, previous studies have reported enhanced uteroplacental blood flow (6) and more favorable redox balance in physically active pregnant women (7), suggesting that exercise may promote a more efficient placental environment.

text.text: Building on this, our group has reported that a supervised concurrent exercise program during pregnancy is associated with greater placental and neonatal weight and shorter labor duration, collectively supporting beneficial effects on placental development and function (8).

text.text: The placenta plays a pivotal role in regulating nutrient transport, endocrine signaling and redox balance (9), and in mediating maternal and fetal physiological adaptations to exercise (10).
text.formatted: The placenta plays a pivotal role in regulating nutrient transport, endocrine signaling and redox balance <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(9)</ref>, and in mediating maternal and fetal physiological adaptations to exercise <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(10)</ref>.

text.text: Collectively, these findings support the concept of the placenta as an exercise-responsive organ.

Nonetheless, the molecular pathways potentially involved in placental adaptations associated with maternal exercise remain poorly understood, with only few studies investigating placental proteins involved in metabolic regulation, oxidative stress, or cellular ageing (10, 11).
text.formatted: Nonetheless, the molecular pathways potentially involved in placental adaptations associated with maternal exercise remain poorly understood, with only few studies investigating placental proteins involved in metabolic regulation, oxidative stress, or cellular ageing <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11)</ref>.

text.text: Identifying molecular pathways associated with these adaptations may improve understanding of how prenatal exercise contributes to maternal-fetal health.
In the search for molecular mediators potentially involved in these adaptations, α-Klotho (hereafter referred to as Klotho) has emerged as a molecule of particular interest.
Klotho is a transmembrane and soluble protein with broad endocrine, paracrine and autocrine actions, originally identified as an anti-aging factor (12).
text.formatted: Klotho is a transmembrane and soluble protein with broad endocrine, paracrine and autocrine actions, originally identified as an anti-aging factor <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(12)</ref>.

text.text: It regulates phosphatevitamin D metabolism and modulates signaling pathways related to oxidative stress and inflammation (13), and has recognized vasculoprotective and renoprotective effects (14, 15).
text.formatted: It regulates phosphatevitamin D metabolism and modulates signaling pathways related to oxidative stress and inflammation <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(13)</ref>, and has recognized vasculoprotective and renoprotective effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(14,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15)</ref>.

text.text: Regular exercise training increases circulating Klotho concentrations in both healthy and clinical populations (16), supporting its role as a potential exerkine mediating systemic benefits of physical exercise.
text.formatted: Regular exercise training increases circulating Klotho concentrations in both healthy and clinical populations <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(16)</ref>, supporting its role as a potential exerkine mediating systemic benefits of physical exercise.

text.text: More recently, Klotho expression has also been demonstrated in human placental tissue, and alterations in its placental or circulating levels have been associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes.

Reduced placental or circulating Klotho concentrations have been described in obstetric disorders associated with placental insufficiency such as intrauterine growth restriction (17) and preeclampsia (18), suggesting that Klotho could contribute to placental homeostasis.
text.formatted: Reduced placental or circulating Klotho concentrations have been described in obstetric disorders associated with placental insufficiency such as intrauterine growth restriction <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(17)</ref> and preeclampsia <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(18)</ref>, suggesting that Klotho could contribute to placental homeostasis.

text.text: Despite this emerging evidence, the regulation of placental Klotho expression remains . poorly understood.

In particular, whether placental Klotho concentrations are associated with prenatal exercise has not been previously investigated, representing an important gap in understanding the molecular pathways through which maternal physical activity may influence placental function.
We hypothesised that participation in a supervised prenatal exercise program would be associated with higher placental Klotho concentrations.
Therefore, the primary aim of this study was to examine the association between participation in a supervised concurrent exercise program during pregnancy and placental Klotho concentrations.
A secondary aim was to assess whether this response differed by fetal sex, given the recognized sexual dimorphism in placental adaptations to maternal stimuli (19).

text.text: >Material and methods
text.formatted: <head n="2." >Material and methods</head>

text.text: This study corresponds to the PLACENTRAINING project, conducted within the framework of the GESTAFIT quasi-randomized trial (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT02582567).
The full methodology of the GESTAFIT quasi-randomized trial has been previously reported (20).
text.formatted: The full methodology of the GESTAFIT quasi-randomized trial has been previously reported <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(20)</ref>.

text.text: Briefly, 384 pregnant women were initially approached at their first routine obstetric visit (around the 12 th gestational week) at the "San Cecilio" and "Virgen de las Nieves" University Hospitals in Granada (southern Spain).
Of these, 159 women met the inclusion criteria (Supplementary Table S1) and provided written informed consent.
text.formatted: Of these, 159 women met the inclusion criteria (Supplementary Table <ref type="table">S1</ref>) and provided written informed consent.

text.text: For the specific objectives of the present study, 76 women with available placental samples and clinical data were analyzed (n=35 control, n=41 exercise).
A flowchart detailing participant enrollment, allocation, follow-up, and the derivation of the final analytical sample is provided in Supplementary Figure S1.
text.formatted: A flowchart detailing participant enrollment, allocation, follow-up, and the derivation of the final analytical sample is provided in Supplementary Figure <ref type="figure">S1</ref>.

text.text: The trial was approved by the Clinical Research Ethics Committee of Granada (Regional Government of Andalusia, Spain; code GESFIT-0448-N-15; approval date: May 19 th , 2015).
The sample size of the parent GESTAFIT trial was calculated a priori to detect differences in gestational weight gain (n = 52) (20).
text.formatted: The sample size of the parent GESTAFIT trial was calculated a priori to detect differences in gestational weight gain (n = 52) <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(20)</ref>.

text.text: No specific sample size calculation was performed for the placental outcomes analyzed in the present study, as these analyses were exploratory in nature and based on the availability of placental tissue samples.
The GESTAFIT trial was originally conceived as a randomized controlled study (20).
text.formatted: The GESTAFIT trial was originally conceived as a randomized controlled study <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(20)</ref>.

text.text: However, during recruitment, participants' preferences regarding participation in supervised exercise precluded strict random allocation.
Consequently, a quasirandomized, preference-informed allocation approach was adopted, as described previously (20).
text.formatted: Consequently, a quasirandomized, preference-informed allocation approach was adopted, as described previously <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(20)</ref>.

text.text: Women who agreed to participate in supervised exercise were assigned to the exercise group, whereas those who declined structured exercise received usual care.
To ensure adequate group balance, additional participants were recruited for the control group.
All participants were followed prospectively and completed the same assessment protocol irrespective of group assignment.

Staff involved in maternal assessments and laboratory analyses, including placental tissue processing and Klotho quantification, were blinded to group allocation, and all statistical analyses were conducted using anonymised datasets.
The overall assessment procedures are summarized in Figure S2.
text.formatted: The overall assessment procedures are summarized in Figure <ref type="figure">S2</ref>.

text.text: Women in the exercise group completed a supervised, structured concurrent training program (aerobic and resistance exercise) from the 17 th gestational week until birth.
Sessions were held three times per week, lasted approximately one hour, and were delivered in small groups by exercise professionals with specific expertise in prenatal exercise prescription.

Each session followed a consistent structure, including a gradual warm-up, a central phase consisting of continuous moderate-intensity aerobic exercises, monitored through heart rate and perceived exertion followed by a resistance-training circuit targeting major muscle groups, and a cool-down incorporating mobility and breathing exercises.
Intensity targets were adjusted individually to remain within recommended ranges for pregnancy.
Attendance was recorded at every session to monitor adherence.
Participants who attended at least 75% of the scheduled sessions were classified as compliant and included in per-protocol analyses.
Additional details are provided elsewhere (21).
text.formatted: Additional details are provided elsewhere <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(21)</ref>.

text.text: During the intervention, women allocated to the exercise group also received seven brief educational talks on healthy pregnancy, including general recommendations on lifestyle and maternal well-being (Appendix A, Supplementary Material).
Participants provided baseline information through self-administered questionnaires.
The variables collected included maternal age, educational level, working status, smoking habit and cohabitation with a partner.
All data were collected prior to the start of the intervention using identical procedures in both study groups.

Information on previous obstetric history was obtained from the official "Pregnancy Health Document", which is a standardized medical record provided to all pregnant women by the regional health system in Andalusia.
This document contains comprehensive obstetric and gynaecological information and was reviewed for research purposes.
Data extracted included gravidity, parity, outcomes of previous pregnancies, past births, and relevant gynaecological antecedents.
Gestational age was estimated based on the date of the last menstrual period (assuming a 28-day cycle) and corrected by ultrasound measurements when required.
Maternal body composition was assessed at the 16 th gestational week following standardized procedures.
Weight was measured with a scale (InBody R20, Biospace, Seoul, Korea), with participants wearing light clothing and no shoes.
Height was recorded using a stadiometer (Seca22, Hamburg, Germany).
Body mass index (BMI) at the 16 th gestational week was calculated as measured weight (kg) divided by height squared (m²).
All measurements were performed by trained personnel using identical protocols in both study groups.

Clinical birth-related information was obtained from the partogram and obstetric records, including gestational age at birth, mode of birth (spontaneous vaginal, instrumental, or caesarean section), newborn sex, birthweight, and duration of labor.
For each placenta, samples were thawed under controlled conditions, and approximately 100 mg of tissue were obtained from a standardized biopsy location.

The assay has a reported sensitivity of 56.25 pg/ml, and no significant crossreactivity or interference with Klotho-related proteins has been described by the manufacturer.

text.text: Briefly, frozen placental biopsies were homogenized in radioimmunoprecipitation assay (RIPA) buffer supplemented with protease inhibitors.
Homogenates were centrifuged, and supernatants were collected and stored at -80 °C until analysis.
Total protein concentration was determined using the Bradford assay, and samples were normalized prior to biomarker quantification.

Placental concentrations of fibroblast growth factor 2 (FGF-2), granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF), platelet-derived growth factor AA (PDGF-AA), tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α), and monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1) were quantified using a customized multiplex magnetic bead-based immunoassay (Luminex xMAP technology; MilliporeSigma, Darmstadt, Germany), according to the manufacturer's instructions.
Data acquisition was performed on a Luminex 200 analyzer using xPONENT software.
Biomarker concentrations were calculated from fiveparameter logistic standard curves and expressed relative to total protein content.
Descriptive statistics were computed for all study variables.
Continuous variables are presented as mean ± standard deviation, and categorical variables as absolute and relative frequencies.
Normality was assessed using graphical methods, including histograms and Q-Q plots, together with the inspection of standardized residuals.

Placental Klotho concentrations showed the presence of extreme influential values; therefore, a winsorization procedure at ±2.58 standard deviations was applied to reduce the influence of outliers while retaining all observations.
This approach improved distributional properties and was considered appropriate for biomarker data.
Between-group differences in participant characteristics were assessed using independent-samples t tests or chi-square tests, as appropriate.

To evaluate associations between participation in the exercise program and placental Klotho concentrations, unadjusted group differences were initially examined using a one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA).

Subsequently, adjusted analyses were performed using analysis of covariance (ANCOVA), including a priori covariates selected based on biological plausibility and previous literature: maternal age, body mass index measured at week 16 . of gestation as an indicator of early-pregnancy adiposity, and mode of birth (cesarean vs vaginal).
Estimated marginal means, unstandardized coefficients (B), 95% confidence intervals, p-values, and partial eta squared (η² ) were reported.
Sex-stratified analyses ₚ were then performed by repeating the adjusted ANCOVA models within strata of fetal sex.
Graphical representations (violin plots) were generated to illustrate sex-dependent patterns.

Given the relevance of placental weight as a surrogate marker of placental growth and functional capacity, an exploratory analysis was conducted to examine its association with placental Klotho concentrations.
Unadjusted associations were first evaluated, followed by adjusted linear models including the same covariates as the primary analysis.

text.text: A total of 76 pregnant women were included in the analyses (mean age 33.2 ± 4.6 years, BMI 24.8 ± 4.1 kg/m² at 16 th gestational week).
Sociodemographic and clinical characteristics of the participants are shown in Table 1.

text.text: Most participants lived with a partner, and approximately two-thirds had completed university education.
Smoking during early pregnancy was uncommon, and around 60% of women were nulliparous.
Regarding birth outcomes, most births were vaginal, with a mean gestational age at birth of 40 weeks.

Mean placental weight was approximately 567 g, with slightly higher values observed in the exercise group compared with the control group, although this difference did not reach statistical significance.
Adherence to the supervised program was high, with an average attendance of 85%.

text.text: Placental Klotho concentrations were significantly higher in the exercise group compared with the control.
As shown in Figure 1, the distribution of Klotho levels was shifted toward higher values in women assigned to the exercise program.

text.text: After adjusting for maternal age, BMI at 16 th gestational week, and mode of birth, placental Klotho concentrations were approximately 101 pg/mL higher in the exercise compared with the control group (B = 100.9, 95% CI 156.9 to 44.9, p = 0.001), corresponding to a moderate effect size (partial η² = 0.164).
None of the included covariates were independently associated with placental Klotho concentrations.
Sex-stratified models revealed a consistent pattern, with higher placental Klotho concentrations in the exercise group for both male and female neonates (Table 2).

text.text: Among male fetuses, adjusted placental Klotho concentrations were higher in the exercise group compared to controls (368.3 ± 27.3 vs.
281.9 ± 28.9 pg/mL), with an adjusted mean difference of 86.4 pg/mL (95% CI 4.7 to 168.2, p = 0.039).
Similarly, among female fetuses, placental Klotho concentrations were higher in the exercise group (367.2 ± 28.4 vs.
246.7 ± 32.0 pg/mL in controls), corresponding to an adjusted mean difference of 120.5 pg/mL (95% CI 32.3 to 208.7, p = 0.009).

The direction and magnitude of the association were broadly comparable across sexes, with no evidence that fetal sex materially modified the association between exercise-group allocation and placental Klotho concentrations.

text.text: To reduce the risk of multiple testing and exploratory bias, analyses were restricted to biomarkers with biologically plausible relevance and adequate data quality, defined by sufficient detectability and sample size.
Unadjusted linear regression models revealed several biomarkers showing significant associations with Klotho, including FGF-2, G-CSF, PDGF-AA, TNF-α and MCP-1.

When each biomarker was subsequently examined in adjusted models controlling for exercise group, FGF-2, G-CSF, PDGF-AA, and TNF-α remained independently associated with placental Klotho concentrations, whereas the association with MCP-1 was no longer statistically significant.
We then explored the potential association between placental weight and placental Klotho concentrations (Table S2).

text.text: Placental weight showed a small and non-significant inverse association with Klotho concentrations in unadjusted analysis.

However, in adjusted models including maternal age, BMI, and mode of birth, placental weight emerged as an independent predictor, such that each additional gram of placental tissue was associated with slightly lower Klotho concentration (B = -0.52, 95% CI -0.85 to -0.19, p = 0.002).
Despite statistical significance, the magnitude of this association was modest.

In this study, women who participated in a supervised concurrent exercise program during pregnancy exhibited higher concentrations of placental Klotho at term birth.

The magnitude of this difference suggests a potentially meaningful association between prenatal exercise and Klotho-related pathways involved in the regulation of oxidative stress, angiogenic signaling, and inflammatory responses.

These findings broaden the current understanding of how structured exercise may influence placental biology, indicating that exercise-related adaptations extend beyond vascular and metabolic domains to include proteins involved in cytoprotection and cellular resilience.
To the best of our knowledge, no previous studies have examined whether maternal exercise modulates Klotho expression in the human placenta.

While prior research has documented multiple placental adaptations to exercise, including increased capillary volume and exchange surface (22), enhanced mitochondrial function (23), and alterations in angiogenic balance or villous structure in physically active women (22, 24, 25), evidence regarding the regulation of proteins directly involved in redox balance and cellular longevity has remained limited.

text.text: In this context, our findings extend existing evidence and align with human studies showing that regular exercise increases Klotho levels in circulating compartments and, in some cases, in peripheral tissues such as skeletal muscle (26) (27) (28).

text.text: Collectively, these data support the biological plausibility that exercise during gestation may activate molecular pathways with cytoprotective potential in placental cells.
The sex-stratified analyses further refine this interpretation.

Although women assigned to the exercise intervention displayed higher placental Klotho concentrations regardless of fetal sex, the magnitude of the association appeared numerically greater in female placentas.
At the same time, baseline Klotho concentrations tended to be higher in males, a pattern that is broadly consistent with the recognized sexual dimorphism in placental physiology (29).

text.text: Specifically, male placentas often exhibit higher metabolic activity and heightened stress responsiveness, whereas female placentas are thought to display greater adaptive plasticity in response to favorable or adverse maternal conditions (30).
text.formatted: Specifically, male placentas often exhibit higher metabolic activity and heightened stress responsiveness, whereas female placentas are thought to display greater adaptive plasticity in response to favorable or adverse maternal conditions <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(30)</ref>.

text.text: Our results suggest that placental Klotho may follow a sex-dimorphic baseline pattern, while its responsiveness to maternal exercise is largely conserved across sexes.

Importantly, the absence of a significant sex-by-group interaction, together with overlapping confidence intervals, indicates that the association between exercise-group allocation and placental Klotho concentrations appears broadly sex-independent.
Nevertheless, the modest differences observed between male and female strata may point to subtle sex-specific regulatory features that warrant confirmation in larger, adequately powered studies.
Exploratory analyses provide additional insight into factors potentially linked to placental Klotho regulation.
Placental weight emerged as a modest but independent predictor of placental Klotho concentrations.

As placental weight is commonly used as a surrogate marker of placental growth and function, this modest inverse association may reflect subtle differences in placental maturation or efficiency and should be interpreted cautiously as hypothesis-generating.
More consistent associations were observed between placental Klotho concentrations and placental biomarkers (full regression models are provided in Supplementary Table S3).

text.text: The positive correlations with FGF-2 and PDGF-AA are consistent with Klotho's proposed role in vascular and tissue homeostasis (12), whereas the association with TNF-α may reflect shared regulatory pathways or compensatory responses to inflammatory signaling, given Klotho's involvement in the modulation of inflammatory and oxidative stress-related pathways (12, 31).

text.text: In the same study population and exercise protocol (32), our group has previously reported that prenatal exercise modulates key placental inflammatory and angiogenic markers, including higher G-CSF levels and lower epidermal growth factor and interleukin-1 receptor antagonist concentrations in the exercise group, as well as sex-specific effects on granulocyte colony-stimulating factor, tumor necrosis factor alpha, and interleukin-6 (21).

text.text: Within this context, the observed associations between placental Klotho and inflammatory and angiogenic markers suggest that Klotho does not act in isolation but is integrated within a broader placental signaling milieu shaped by maternal exercise.
These findings are consistent with our previous report in the same cohort showing exerciseinduced modulation of placental inflammatory and angiogenic markers.
Several biological mechanisms may plausibly contribute to the higher placental Klotho concentrations observed in women who exercise during pregnancy.

Klotho is a key regulator of oxidative stress, inflammatory signaling and cellular metabolism, and its expression increases under conditions of improved mitochondrial function and reduced cellular stress (12).

text.text: Prenatal exercise has been proposed to enhance placental antioxidant capacity and to support mitochondrial adaptations, as suggested by recent experimental and review studies (33) (34) (35), while also modulating cytokine and growth factor profiles toward a more anti-inflammatory and pro-angiogenic milieu (21).

text.text: Furthermore, exercise-induced increases in uteroplacental perfusion may expose placental cells to altered mechanical forces, such as shear stress, which are recognized regulators of endothelial and trophoblast biology (36, 37).

text.text: Although direct evidence linking shear stress to Klotho regulation in human placental tissue is currently lacking, these converging pathways support a biologically coherent framework in which prenatal exercise may create a placental microenvironment conducive to Klotho upregulation.

Given the central role of Klotho in oxidative balance, vascular health and cellular resilience, these results provide a novel perspective on the molecular pathways through which prenatal exercise may contribute to placental and fetal well-being.

Future studies should aim to elucidate the upstream mechanisms regulating placental Klotho expression in placental tissue and determine whether exercise-induced modulation of placental Klotho translates into clinically meaningful benefits for both the mother and offspring.
Some limitations should be acknowledged.

The quasi-randomized design, although pragmatic, may be associated with residual selection bias related to participants' exercise preferences, despite prospective follow-up and generally comparable baseline characteristics between groups.

This limitation reflects a common methodological and ethical barrier in antenatal exercise research, where participant preferences and feasibility constraints frequently preclude full randomization (38).
text.formatted: This limitation reflects a common methodological and ethical barrier in antenatal exercise research, where participant preferences and feasibility constraints frequently preclude full randomization <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(38)</ref>.

text.text: The sample size, while sufficient to detect between-group differences in placental Klotho concentrations, limits the precision of sex-specific estimates and reduces statistical power to formally test interaction effects.
In addition, the absence of direct assessment of placental perfusion and shear stress precludes definitive conclusions regarding the mechanistic pathways underlying the observed associations.
Despite these limitations, the present study has important strengths.

It is the first study, to our knowledge, to examine the influence of a prenatal exercise program on placental Klotho concentration, providing novel molecular insight into how maternal physical activity may shape placental biology.
The use of a supervised and well-characterized concurrent exercise intervention with objective monitoring of adherence (85%), enhances internal validity.
Finally, the incorporation of sex-stratified analyses adds valuable information regarding the potential role of fetal sex in placental molecular adaptations to maternal exercise.
A supervised concurrent exercise program during pregnancy is associated with higher placental Klotho concentrations, with findings across both male and female fetuses.

These findings support the rationale for further translational research aimed at determining whether Klotho could serve as a biomarker of placental responsiveness to lifestyle interventions, or potentially contribute to strategies for optimizing prenatal care.
